analysis.one_liner: Stops insurers and Medicare drug plans from gagging pharmacies about cheaper ways to buy medicine.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, despite bipartisan sponsorship from Rep. Erik Paulsen and Rep. Anna Eshoo.
analysis.plain_summary: Many health plans and Medicare drug plans stop pharmacies from telling customers that paying cash for a prescription could cost less than using their insurance. This bill would make it illegal for insurers, group health plans, Medicare Advantage plans, and Medicare drug plan sponsors to ban or punish pharmacies for sharing that information. It would also require pharmacies to explain what paying cash means for a customer's deductible and report cash purchases back to the plan, and it directs a federal study of how common these gag rules are.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance and seniors in Medicare drug plans who might pay less out of pocket for a prescription by paying cash instead of using their benefits. Pharmacies would also gain the freedom to tell customers about cheaper options without risking their contract with the plan.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits health insurers and group health plans from barring pharmacies from disclosing, or financially penalizing pharmacies for disclosing, cheaper alternative ways to buy a drug, such as paying the cash price.
Applies the same prohibition to Medicare Advantage organizations and Medicare prescription drug plan sponsors, the plans covering most seniors' drug benefits.

Requires pharmacies that disclose a cheaper cash option to also tell the customer what paying cash would do to their deductible, so people can make an informed choice, and to report cash purchases back to the plan.
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to study and report to Congress on how widespread these pharmacy gag prohibitions are among plans and insurers.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, Medicare Advantage insurers, and drug plan sponsors, which would lose a tool for steering customers toward plan-benefit purchases and could see more claims paid outside the plan's cost-sharing structure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and Medicare drug plans

drawbacks.text: The new protections do not take effect automatically. They only apply after the Secretary determines that a plan or insurer is actually using a gag rule, which means the ban depends on federal enforcement action before it protects anyone.

Paying cash instead of using benefits generally does not count toward a plan deductible, so a customer who saves money on one prescription could lose progress toward coverage they need later. The bill requires pharmacies to warn customers of this, but does not fix it.
Pharmacies that disclose cheaper cash options must report the amount paid back to the plan, adding a compliance and reporting duty on pharmacies that could affect how they handle such disclosures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but modest: it removes a barrier to honest pricing conversations at the pharmacy counter, which can save individual customers money on specific prescriptions. The main design weakness is the conditional trigger — the ban only activates if federal regulators first find a plan using a gag rule, which could delay or dilute the protection. Overall a consumer-friendly, low-cost bill whose biggest limitation is how narrow it is.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Erik Paulsen introduced the bill on July 31, 2018, with Rep. Anna Eshoo as a cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On August 3, 2018, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and again on August 17, 2018, to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, Medicare Advantage insurers, and drug plan sponsors keep the ability to restrict what pharmacies tell customers about cheaper prices. Consumers who might have saved by paying cash see no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and Medicare drug plan sponsors

for.name: Rep. Erik Paulsen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COST Act to bar plans from restricting what pharmacies can tell customers about cheaper drug prices.

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on August 3, 2018, and took no further action — no hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over Medicare provisions
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on August 17, 2018, and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and its one cosponsor was a Democrat, so support was bipartisan; its death in committee was a matter of committees never acting rather than a party-bloc vote, and the record contains no opposition votes or statements.

industries.industry: Health insurers, Medicare Advantage insurers, and Medicare drug plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill would bar these plans from prohibiting or penalizing pharmacies for telling customers about cheaper cash prices, and from using financial disincentives to enforce that silence. Their gain from such rules is customers paying full plan prices when cash would be cheaper, so their interest runs against the consumer's.

Pharmacies would gain the freedom to tell customers when paying cash costs less than using their insurance, without risking penalties like reduced payments or increased utilization review. The bill also adds a duty on pharmacies to report cash purchases to plans and explain deductible effects.
